1 · External earth fault loop impedance (Ze)

Measured at the origin with the installation isolated and the main earthing conductor disconnected. For TN these are the distributor's typical maximums, and what the BS 7671 tables assume. TT is different — the return is through your own electrode, so 21 Ω is a working ceiling you confirm by measurement.

{% for z in ze %}
{{ z.system }}
{{ z.max }} Ω
{{ z.note }}
{% endfor %}
Not a statutory cap. Typical maximums for supplies up to 100 A. Ze must be measured and recorded at every installation — if your reading exceeds it, query the DNO.

2 · How Ze and Zs relate

Zs = Ze + (R1 + R2)

Ze is what the supply brings to your origin; (R₁+R₂) is what your circuit adds. Zs is the total the device sees under an earth fault — and it is Zs that must not exceed the tabulated maximum.

4 · Reading the tables on sheets 2 and 3

Every figure on sheets 2 and 3 is the BS 7671 tabulated maximum, derived with Cmin = 0.95 — as printed in the Regulations, nothing pre-corrected. Cmin is the minimum voltage factor for variation in time and place and for transformer tap changes; for an LV supply under the ESQCR it takes the value 0.95 (Reg 253.0, Reg 543.4). So a Type B 32 A is 230 × 0.95 ÷ (5 × 32) = 1.37 Ω. At Cmin = 1.0 it would read 1.44 Ω — if your reference shows that, it is not the BS 7671 figure.
Temperature — and this is where most people trip up.
The tabulated values assume conductors at their operating temperature (70 °C for thermoplastic; NOTE 2 to Tables 41.2–41.4). You measure cold, so BS 7671 sets a separate acceptance criterion in Appendix 3. Regulation 411.4.4 (or 411.5.4) is met when:
Zs(measured) < 0.8 × U0 ÷ (Ia × Cmin)   — in practice, 0.8 × the tabulated figure
GN3 1.16.9 restates it, which is why it gets called "the GN3 factor" — but it is BS 7671's own criterion, not merely guidance.
⚠️ The 0.8 is NOT applied anywhere in this document. Apply it yourself whenever you compare a cold measurement.

5 · Worked example

StepWorkingResult
32 A Type B RCBO on TN-C-S — measured ZeWithin the 0.35 Ω typical maximum0.28 Ω
Measured Zs at the furthest pointSo (R1+R2) = 1.12 − 0.281.12 Ω
Tabulated maximumSheet 2, Type B, 32 A1.37 Ω
Against the tabulated figure1.12 Ω < 1.37 ΩComplies
Against Appendix 3 (cold measurement)0.8 × 1.37 = 1.10 Ω, and 1.12 Ω > 1.10 ΩDoes not
That last pair of rows is the whole point of this sheet. 1.12 Ω sits inside the tabulated 1.37 Ω but outside the 1.10 Ω Appendix 3 accepts for a cold measurement — so a reading that looks compliant against the table does not meet BS 7671's criterion. Compare like for like, every time, before you write C1, C2 or a tick.

Type B and Type C carry one row each — the figure satisfies both the 0.4 s and the 5 s disconnection time. Type D is the only curve with two: it trips at 20×In for 0.4 s but 10×In is enough for 5 s, so the 5 s values are exactly double. That is a genuine shared formula with Type C, not a misprint.

BS 3871-1 circuit-breakers Types 1, 2, 3 and 4

BS 3871-1 is withdrawn, superseded by BS EN 60898 — which is exactly why you need this table on an EICR: these devices are still in service in a great many older boards. Types 1–4 are not interchangeable with B/C/D. A Type 1 trips at 4×In where a Type B trips at 5×In, so recording an old Type 1 as a "Type B" understates its permitted Zs by 20% and can fail a circuit that complies. BS 7671 no longer tabulates these; the figures below follow the IET On-Site Guide.

RCDs BS 7671 Table 41.5 · Reg 411.5.3

Where disconnection is by residual current rather than overcurrent, the limit is UL ÷ IΔn, with UL = 50 V.

{% for r in rcd %}{% endfor %}{% for r in rcd %}{% endfor %}
IΔn{{ r.ma }} mA
Maximum Zs (Ω){{ r.max }}
An RCBO is not an RCD for this purpose. It has its own overcurrent element, so its Zs comes from Table 41.3 — a Type B 32 A RCBO is 1.37 Ω, exactly the same as the MCB. The 50/IΔn limit governs only where a standalone RCD (BS EN 61008) provides the fault protection. ⚠️ Note 2 to Table 41.5 advises that the installation earth electrode resistance should be as low as practicable, and that a value exceeding 200 Ω may not be stable — soil dries and freezes. That is advice about stability, not a permitted maximum.
